title: oekaki overlay
description:
A list of assertions about a graph, each carrying provenance. Written by a human reading an operations console, or by a model reading one for them; never written by oekaki, which only consumes it. That boundary is what keeps the tool deterministic while allowing non-deterministic input: the overlay is a file, and identical files still produce identical bytes.

Deliberately a separate document from the IR rather than a superset of it. A model asked to emit an IR has to get axes, groups, group paths and referential integrity right; a useful assertion here is six lines. Orthogonality is the single biggest lever on how often a generated overlay is valid.

kind.description: Identifies this as an overlay rather than a graph, so one command can accept both and tell the user which it got.

version.description: Overlay vocabulary version, versioned independently of the IR. The IR freezes at 1.0; this vocabulary needs to keep moving well past that, and two things with different freeze dates should not share a version number.

metadata.description: Defaults and provenance for the whole document.

origin.description: Who wrote this, used as the default for every assertion that does not say. Repeating "origin" on fifty assertions is fifty chances to typo it.

window.description: The period this document's observations cover, in the author's own words, e.g. "last-7d". Echoed into the graph and drawn with the diagram: saying "blind spot" without saying over what period is a lie of omission. Never parsed, never compared to a clock.

sinks.description: Log destinations this document refers to. A sink that corresponds to a resource already in the graph attaches to it; one that does not becomes a node of its own, so a destination nobody modelled still appears.

id.description: Local handle, referenced by this document's assertions.

name.description: What the destination is called where it lives.

assertions.description: The claims. A flat array with a uniform envelope, nested no more than two levels deep, so that there is nowhere to put an object in the wrong place.

selector.description: Names something in the graph without knowing its IR id. Keys are tried in a fixed precedence, and several identity keys given together must all match — a workload name in one namespace is not the same workload as that name in another.

node.description: An exact node id. If given and not found, resolution stops: somebody who typed an id meant that id.

type.description: A resource type, used with name.

name.description: A resource's short name. The weakest key, and frequently ambiguous — which is reported rather than guessed at.

assert.description: logs.declared: configuration promises this subject ships logs to a sink. logs.observed: logs from this subject were actually seen. logs.none: somebody looked and found no destination — a claim, not an absence, which is what makes a blind spot distinguishable from an unchecked resource. edge: a connection exists that no parser found. edge.suppress: a connection a parser found is not real. note: somebody wrote something about this subject, in Markdown. It is kept beside the graph with their name on it rather than folded into the resource, because the sentence is theirs and not the estate's. node: something exists, or is called something, that is in no input file. A type says what it is, a name says what to call it, and either alone is a claim worth making: renaming a resource the parser did find is the same act as adopting one it did not. path: a route somebody means a request to take, written down as a walk of selectors. It is the declared side of the comparison a path listing makes, and it is preferred over the routes derived by following references — which is the whole reason to write one down.

sink.description: Id of a sink declared in this document.

records.description: How many were seen. Zero is a finding; omitting it means no count was available.

kind.description: Which family of evidence this is. For edge and edge.suppress, the edge kind. For path, which kind of declared route it is: it defaults to iac_ref and may not be observed, because what a person writes down is a claim about what may happen and what did happen comes from something that watched it.

type.description: Resource type, for a node assertion. Required unless a name is given.

name.description: Display name, for a node assertion. Required unless a type is given.

text.description: What was written, for a note assertion. Markdown, as typed.

through.description: The walk a route assertion declares, in order. Each participant is a selector, resolved by the same ladder as every other subject here, because a person writing a route down knows it as "the checkout service" rather than as a Terraform address. The walk is applied whole or not at all: a participant the unmatched policy drops ends the assertion, because a walk with a hop missing is a different walk.

label.description: What to call a route in a listing, when somebody has a name for it better than its ends.

via.description: How the claimant knew, in their own words.

origin.description: Overrides the document's origin for this assertion.

kind.$comment: A route written down is a route somebody means, not one anything watched. Refused here as well as in Go so the message names the JSON path.
